questions.question: A legislature passes a statute that a judge finds impossible to square with the federal charter. Invoking Article VI, the judge will treat the statute as:
questions.correctAnswer: Void wherever it clashes with the Constitution, which outranks it
distractors: The state law controls because states are closer to the people
Both laws apply equally until Congress chooses one
The governor decides which law to enforce
questions.explanation: Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws and treaties 'the supreme Law of the Land.' Judges in every state are bound by it, any state law to the contrary notwithstanding - the principle the Supreme Court applied in cases from McCulloch to Cooper v. Aaron.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: When laws collide, the Constitution wins - Article VI.

questions.question: Which principle divides power between the national government and the states?
questions.correctAnswer: Federalism
distractors: Separation of powers
Judicial review
Popular sovereignty
questions.explanation: Federalism splits sovereignty between two levels of government, each acting directly on the people. Separation of powers is different - it divides authority among branches at the same level.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federalism splits levels; separation splits branches.

questions.question: The power to coin money is denied to the states. It is an example of a power that is:
questions.correctAnswer: Exclusive to the national government
distractors: Reserved to the states under the Tenth Amendment
Concurrent, shared by both levels
Held only by the Federal Reserve's regional banks
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 10 forbids states to coin money or emit bills of credit. Exclusive federal powers like coining money, declaring war and conducting foreign policy mark the outer frame of federalism.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One money for one union: coining is federal only.

questions.question: A state requires candidates for its own legislature to hold a college degree. The strongest constitutional objection is:
questions.correctAnswer: The qualifications for office are fixed by the governing constitution and cannot be enlarged by ordinary statute
distractors: The First Amendment's freedom of the press
The ban on bills of attainder in all cases
The Full Faith and Credit Clause
questions.explanation: By analogy to Powell v. McCormack and U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton, the qualifications listed in the controlling constitution are exclusive. A legislature may not add to them by statute; only a constitutional amendment can.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Listed qualifications are the whole list.

questions.question: Which action is an example of a check the judicial branch holds over the executive?
questions.correctAnswer: Declaring an executive action unconstitutional in a case before the court
distractors: Vetoing a presidential pardon
Impeaching the president by majority vote
Writing the executive's annual budget
questions.explanation: Courts check the executive through judicial review of actions challenged in real cases - as when the Supreme Court voided President Truman's steel seizure rationale in Youngstown. Impeachment belongs to Congress; the veto belongs to the president.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Courts check presidents by judging their acts in cases.

questions.question: A president signs a treaty, but it takes effect only after:
questions.correctAnswer: The Senate gives its advice and consent by a two-thirds vote
distractors: The House votes by simple majority
The Supreme Court approves the text
A national referendum ratifies it
questions.explanation: Article II lodges treaty consent in the Senate alone, by supermajority - a deliberate brake on foreign commitments. Executive agreements, by contrast, rest on the president's own authority or existing statutes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate, not the House.

questions.question: The 'necessary and proper' clause matters most because it:
questions.correctAnswer: Lets Congress choose means to execute its listed powers, as upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland
distractors: Gives states power to nullify federal laws they dislike
Allows the president to legislate in emergencies without Congress
Requires every federal law to be approved by state legislatures
questions.explanation: McCulloch (1819) read the clause broadly: if the end is legitimate and within the Constitution, means that are appropriate and not prohibited are constitutional. Maryland also could not tax the national bank.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: McCulloch: legitimate ends, chosen means, no state tax on the Union.

questions.question: A city bans all political leafleting on every public sidewalk. A court applying the First Amendment will most likely:
questions.correctAnswer: Strike the ban down - sidewalks are traditional public forums and a total ban on a medium of speech is overbroad
distractors: Uphold it because cities own all sidewalks absolutely
Uphold it because leaflets cause litter in every case
Send the question to a popular referendum
questions.explanation: From Hague v. CIO through Schneider v. State, sidewalks and parks are forums held in trust for speech; anti-litter aims must be pursued by punishing litterers, not by silencing speakers. Content-neutral time, place and manner rules remain possible.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Punish the litterer, not the leaflet.

questions.question: The incorporation doctrine holds that most of the Bill of Rights limits the states because:
questions.correctAnswer: The Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause makes fundamental rights binding on state governments
distractors: The original Bill of Rights always bound the states by its own text
State constitutions copy the federal one automatically
Congress passed a statute incorporating them in 1791
questions.explanation: Barron v. Baltimore (1833) held the Bill of Rights bound only the federal government. Beginning with Gitlow (1925), the Court selectively incorporated most guarantees against the states through the Fourteenth Amendment - completed for the Second Amendment in McDonald (2010).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fourteenth carries the Bill of Rights to the states.

questions.question: A defendant is forced to testify against himself at trial. Which protection is violated?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination
distractors: The Third Amendment quartering ban
The Seventh Amendment jury right in civil cases
The Tenth Amendment reserved powers
questions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment provides that no person 'shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself.' Miranda warnings grew from the same privilege for custodial interrogation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Silence is a right: the Fifth protects it.

questions.question: Gerrymandering is challenged after the 2030 census. Which institution draws congressional district lines in most states?
questions.correctAnswer: The state legislature, subject to state and federal constitutional limits
distractors: The United States Senate, by national committee
The Census Bureau itself
County clerks in each district
questions.explanation: Article I's Elections Clause gives state legislatures the first word on congressional maps; some states assign the task to commissions. Federal courts police racial gerrymanders (Shaw v. Reno) while Rucho (2019) left partisan gerrymandering to the political branches.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Legislatures draw; commissions in some states; courts police race, not party.

questions.question: The 22nd Amendment limits a president to:
questions.correctAnswer: Two elected terms (at most ten years counting a partial term served)
distractors: One term of six years
Three elected terms
Unlimited terms if Congress consents
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1951 after Franklin Roosevelt's four elections, the amendment bars election more than twice - and limits a successor who serves over half of another's term to one election of their own.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two elections, ten years at most: the 22nd.

questions.question: A bill passes the House 260-175 and the Senate 55-45, and the president vetoes it. To become law it now needs:
questions.correctAnswer: Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate voting to override
distractors: A majority of state legislatures to ratify it
The Supreme Court to lift the veto
A new president to sign it within ten days
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 7 sets the override at two-thirds of each chamber. Overrides are rare - roughly 7 percent of regular vetoes in American history - which is why the veto is called the president's strongest legislative weapon.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds, twice: the price of overriding a veto.

questions.question: Which clause of the Fourteenth Amendment was the Supreme Court's main tool in Brown v. Board of Education?
questions.correctAnswer: The Equal Protection Clause
distractors: The Privileges or Immunities Clause
The Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment
The Guarantee Clause of Article IV
questions.explanation: Brown (1954) held state-mandated school segregation inherently unequal under the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause, overturning Plessy's application to public education. The Privileges or Immunities Clause had been narrowed decades earlier in the Slaughter-House Cases.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Equal protection did Brown's work.

questions.question: A state sets a poll tax for its own state elections. After the 24th Amendment and Harper v. Virginia, the tax is:
questions.correctAnswer: Unconstitutional - the 24th bars poll taxes in federal elections and Harper bars them in state elections under equal protection
distractors: Valid, because states control their own elections absolutely
Valid only if the revenue funds schools
Unconstitutional only for voters over 65
questions.explanation: The 24th Amendment (1964) ended poll taxes in federal contests; Harper (1966) held wealth unrelated to voting qualifications in state elections too. Together they closed the poll-tax era at every level.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Poll taxes died twice: the 24th, then Harper.

questions.question: In a federal criminal case, the prosecution must prove guilt:
questions.correctAnswer: Beyond a reasonable doubt, to a unanimous jury in most cases
distractors: By a preponderance of the evidence, like a civil suit
To a majority of six jurors chosen by the judge
By clear evidence to the trial judge alone
questions.explanation: In re Winship (1970) constitutionalized proof beyond a reasonable doubt; Ramos v. Louisiana (2020) required unanimous verdicts for convictions in state criminal trials as well, incorporating the Sixth Amendment jury right.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Reasonable doubt, unanimous jury: Winship and Ramos.

questions.question: An interest group wants to influence a rule being written by the Environmental Protection Agency. Its most direct formal channel is:
questions.correctAnswer: Submitting comments during the notice-and-comment rulemaking process
distractors: Filing an amicus brief with the Supreme Court before any rule exists
Asking a senator to veto the rule by letter
Petitioning the Federal Reserve for a hearing
questions.explanation: The Administrative Procedure Act requires agencies to publish proposed rules and consider public comments. Comment files become part of the record courts review - a quiet but real point of citizen leverage over the bureaucracy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Comment on the rule: the APA's open door.

questions.question: Which statement about political parties in the Constitution is accurate?
questions.correctAnswer: The Constitution never mentions parties; they grew from practice and are regulated largely by state law
distractors: The Constitution creates exactly two official parties
The First Amendment requires states to fund parties equally
Article II assigns the vice presidency to the runner-up party forever
questions.explanation: Washington warned against factions in his Farewell Address even as Federalists and Democratic-Republicans organized. Primaries, ballot access and party rules are creatures of state law within First Amendment limits (as in Tashjian and California Democratic Party v. Jones).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Parties: everywhere in practice, nowhere in the text.

questions.question: A state law requires voters to register 50 days before an election and provides ample registration access. Courts will generally:
questions.correctAnswer: Uphold reasonable, nondiscriminatory registration rules while striking rules that severely burden the right to vote
distractors: Strike all registration deadlines as unconstitutional per se
Require states to allow registration only on election day itself
Transfer registration to the federal government
questions.explanation: Under the Anderson-Burdick balancing test, reasonable election administration survives; severe burdens need compelling justification. The framework explains why deadlines and ID rules are litigated fact by fact rather than by slogan.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Balance the burden: Anderson-Burdick runs election law.

questions.question: The 'shadow docket' criticism of the modern Supreme Court refers to:
questions.correctAnswer: Major decisions made through emergency orders with little briefing or signed reasoning
distractors: The Court's practice of meeting at night in secret
Unsigned dissents in ordinary argued cases
The justices' unpublished travel schedules
questions.explanation: Emergency applications - stays and injunctions - increasingly resolve big questions (election rules, immigration programs) without full merits opinions. Defenders cite urgency; critics cite opacity. The term itself comes from scholar William Baude (2015).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Big rulings, thin reasoning: the shadow docket debate.

questions.correctAnswer: The Tenth Amendment
distractors: The Third Amendment
The Necessary and Proper Clause
The Commerce Clause
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment reserves powers 'not delegated to the United States... nor prohibited' to the states or the people. Police powers - health, safety, morals, land use - live in that reservation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: What is not given or forbidden is reserved: the Tenth.

questions.question: A state legalizes a practice that federal law still prohibits. Under current doctrine, the practical result is:
questions.correctAnswer: Both sovereigns keep their own law: the state cannot be forced to enforce the federal ban, but federal officers may enforce federal law themselves
distractors: The state law automatically repeals the federal law
Federal law disappears in that state by nullification
The state may arrest federal agents for enforcing federal law
questions.explanation: Anti-commandeering doctrine (Printz; Murphy v. NCAA) bars Congress from conscripting state officers, but supremacy still lets federal agents enforce federal statutes. The marijuana era is the standard classroom example of the standoff.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two sovereigns, two laws: neither erases the other.

questions.question: The Full Faith and Credit Clause requires states to:
questions.correctAnswer: Honor the public acts, records and court judgments of other states, with Congress setting the manner of proof
distractors: Accept other states' driver's licenses as professional licenses automatically
Merge their court systems into one national system
Use identical tax rates across state lines
questions.explanation: Article IV, Section 1 underlies everything from enforcing a sister-state judgment to recognizing marriages and adoptions across state lines. Congress's implementing statutes, not the clause alone, settle most modern disputes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Judgments travel: full faith and credit makes states one legal country.

questions.question: A governor is asked to extradite a fugitive to another state but refuses on policy grounds. Under Kentucky v. Dennison's modern replacement, Puerto Rico v. Branstad (1987):
questions.correctAnswer: Extradition of fugitives is a mandatory constitutional duty federal courts may enforce
distractors: The governor's refusal is final and unreviewable
Extradition exists only between states sharing a border
The fugitive may choose which state tries him
questions.explanation: Branstad overruled Dennison's 1861 hands-off rule: Article IV's extradition duty is mandatory and judicially enforceable. Interstate rendition is one of the few state duties federal courts will directly compel.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rendition is a duty, not a favor: Branstad.

questions.question: Direct democracy exists at the federal level in the United States:
questions.correctAnswer: Nowhere - initiative and referendum are state and local devices only
distractors: In the form of national referendums every four years
Through binding online polls run by Congress
In constitutional amendments proposed by petition
questions.explanation: Citizens may pressure Congress but cannot enact or repeal federal law by ballot measure. Initiative, referendum and recall entered American practice through Progressive-era state constitutions - New Mexico's among them, as the state layer of this pack shows.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No national ballot box for laws: direct democracy is a state tool.

questions.question: The Senate's filibuster can be ended on most legislation by cloture, which requires:
questions.correctAnswer: Sixty votes (three-fifths of senators duly chosen and sworn)
distractors: A simple majority of 51 in all cases
Unanimous consent of all 100 senators
The vice president's sole signature
questions.explanation: Rule XXII sets cloture at three-fifths. Carve-outs made by majority precedent - the 'nuclear options' of 2013 and 2017 - lowered the threshold for nominations, leaving 60 as the working number for statutes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sixty to close debate: the filibuster's price.

questions.correctAnswer: Originating revenue bills and bringing impeachment charges

Granting pardons and reprieves
Appointing ambassadors
questions.explanation: Article I gives the House the first move on taxes ('All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House') and the sole power of impeachment; the Senate tries impeachments and handles treaties and confirmations.

questions.question: A president facing a hostile House investigation claims executive privilege over all documents. Under United States v. Nixon (1974):
questions.correctAnswer: A generalized claim of privilege yields to a demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a criminal trial
distractors: Presidential privilege is absolute and never reviewable
Congress may seize any presidential paper at will
The tapes question belonged only to the D.C. Circuit with no Supreme Court role
questions.explanation: The Court recognized a qualified privilege for confidentiality but unanimously ordered the tapes surrendered. Nixon complied and resigned within weeks - the rule of law's sharpest modern test of a president.

questions.question: Standing to sue in federal court requires a plaintiff to show:
questions.correctAnswer: A concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, traceable to the defendant and redressable by the court
distractors: Only strong disagreement with a government policy
Membership in any taxpayer group for any federal spending
A letter of permission from a member of Congress
questions.explanation: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992) states the three elements. Generalized grievances and most taxpayer suits (Frothingham; Flast's narrow exception aside) fail at the courthouse door for lack of standing.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Injury, trace, remedy: Lujan's three keys to the courthouse.

questions.question: The Establishment Clause and the Free Exercise Clause can point in opposite directions. A school that funds clergy-led prayer at graduation violates the first; a law banning students' private prayer violates the second. The pair together aim at:
questions.correctAnswer: Government neutrality toward religion - neither advancing it as an official nor burdening private practice
distractors: A state church supported by taxes in every state
The removal of all religious references from public life
A rule that religious citizens may not hold office
questions.explanation: From Everson and Engel through Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022), the Court has steered between establishment and free-exercise poles, lately emphasizing history, tradition and coercion. Neutrality, not hostility, is the stated lodestar.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Neither advance nor burden: neutrality is the lodestar.

questions.question: Defamation law after New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) requires a public official suing over criticism to prove:
questions.correctAnswer: Actual malice - the statement was made with knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth
distractors: Only that the statement was unkind in tone
Nothing at all; officials win automatically
That the newspaper failed to endorse his campaign
questions.explanation: Sullivan constitutionalized libel to protect 'uninhibited, robust, and wide-open' debate. The actual-malice standard extends to public figures; private figures need at least negligence for fault under Gertz.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Officials must prove actual malice: Sullivan's shield for debate.

questions.question: A warrantless search of a home is presumptively unreasonable. The exception that lets police enter when they see a crime being committed inside an open doorway is:
questions.correctAnswer: Plain view (coupled with exigent circumstances for entry) - contraband or evidence clearly visible from a lawful vantage point
distractors: The good mood exception
A blanket rule that homes are never protected
Consent presumed from owning a doorbell
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment protects the home most strongly (Kyllo; Florida v. Jardines). Plain view justifies seizure of visible contraband; entering requires more - a warrant, consent or true exigency such as hot pursuit (Lange, 2021).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The home is first among equals in the Fourth Amendment.

questions.question: Eminent domain under the Fifth Amendment allows government to take private property only:
questions.correctAnswer: For public use, with just compensation paid to the owner
distractors: For any reason, without payment, if a majority votes for it
From citizens who criticize the government
For private developers in all cases without review
questions.explanation: Kelo v. City of New London (2005) read 'public use' broadly to include economic development - a holding so controversial that most states, New Mexico included, tightened their own laws afterward. Compensation remains non-negotiable.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Public use plus just compensation - and Kelo's backlash.

questions.question: The right to bear arms as an individual right was recognized in:
questions.correctAnswer: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), extended to the states in McDonald (2010) and reframed by Bruen's text-history-tradition test (2022)
distractors: United States v. Miller alone, which settled the question in 1939
The Articles of Confederation
A statute passed by Congress in 1791 and never reviewed
questions.explanation: Heller held the Second Amendment protects an individual's right to possess a handgun in the home. Bruen replaced interest-balancing with a historical-analogue test for modern regulations - the doctrine students now meet first.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Heller, McDonald, Bruen: the modern Second Amendment trilogy.

questions.question: Civil rights statutes like the Civil Rights Act of 1964 rest mainly on which congressional power as applied to private businesses?
questions.correctAnswer: The Commerce Clause, as upheld in Heart of Atlanta Motel and Katzenbach v. McClung
distractors: The Taxing Clause alone, with no other support
The president's pardon power
State police powers delegated to Congress
questions.explanation: Because the Civil Rights Cases (1883) barred Congress from reaching private discrimination under the Fourteenth Amendment alone, the 1964 Act regulated businesses affecting interstate commerce - motels and restaurants included - and the Court upheld it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Commerce carried civil rights where the Fourteenth could not reach.

questions.correctAnswer: Accessibility and occupation-diverse members, at the cost of dependence on executive agencies, lobbyists and interim staff for expertise - a trade the state re-argues every decade, including recent proposals to lengthen sessions and pay salaries
distractors: No challenges of any kind, by universal scholarly agreement
Automatic corruption in every session by definition
A legislature that never needs staff or research
questions.explanation: Reform commissions have repeatedly proposed professionalization; voters and legislators keep the citizen model. The honest civics answer holds both sides: who can afford to serve unpaid is itself a representation question.
